webTitle: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner

fields.headline: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner
fields.trailText: House minority leader is under attack from his own party for ‘affordability crisis’ meeting with president’s son-in-law
fields.bodyText: Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the US House of Representatives, has defended his meeting with Jared Kushner and claimed it was arranged at the request of Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Jeffries, who has come under attack from Democrats since the New York Times reported on Sunday that the two met privately to discuss common ground on issues like housing, immigration and the high cost of living, said he agreed to the meeting “to discuss the affordability crisis” in the US. In an X post on Monday, Jeffries insisted: “No one from the Trump cartel is getting a pass.” “I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.” Jeffries appeared to be referring to actions planned by Democrats should they retake control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections. But in meeting with Kushner – who serves as an envoy for the Trump administration, working on conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran – Jeffries provoked a response from Democrats and Republicans alike. Tommy Vietor, a former Obama aide and co-host of Pod Save America, criticized Kushner, noting that he had “no actual government job” and claiming he “just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals”. Former Clinton strategist James Carville said in an “urgent message to Hakeem Jeffries” that the House minority leader had no business meeting with Kushner. A more appropriate response than meeting to discuss affordability, Carville suggested, would be to “drag his ass” before a congressional committee and grill him on his “backdoor-dealing” with other figures in Trump’s orbit. The Trump administration, family members and cronies “have no idea what they’re doing”, Carville added. “They’re making every backdoor bullshit deal they can. And we don’t meet with them. Don’t meet with them.” New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who opposed a primary challenge to Jeffries’ Brooklyn seat by the city councilman Chi Ossé, was asked if he would still support the representative as House majority leader if Democrats take back the House in November. “I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader,” Mamdani said. Republicans have mostly been more circumspect about the meeting. “I don’t know what that’s about,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, told Fox News’s Peter Doocy on Sunday. “I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on.” “He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House,” Johnson added. In an earlier response to news of the meeting, Jeffries said that he was looking “to stop the madness”, adding that Democrats “have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition”.

webTitle: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’

fields.headline: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’
fields.trailText: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
fields.bodyText: Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the “negative impact” of datacenters amid a growing backlash across the political spectrum. Paxton, endorsed by Donald Trump but facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a “Texas first” datacenter plan on X with a graphic that the social media network flagged as “Made with AI”. Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November’s US midterm elections. An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents. Last year Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the “epicenter of AI development”, but on Sunday he told ABC’s This Week program that tech companies “basically dug their own grave for the problem that’s been caused for them and that’s why they got the backlash they deserve”. On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general in Texas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children’s safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans’ electricity bills. He also pledged to support Abbott’s state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas’s electricity capacity rather than taking from it. Paxton said in a statement: “Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods. “This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children.” The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn in a Republican primary runoff, to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talarico has urged tighter regulations on datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies. Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: “Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans’ requests to block datacenter development in their communities. “Now he’s scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he’s making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make.” The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Report describes the election as a toss-up. Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs. Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last year championed a $20bn investment by Amazon but last week signed an executive order he said imposes the “strictest guardrails in the nation”. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont, has urged big tech leaders to pause AI development. The Axios website reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party’s chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio. Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. He told Punchbowl News recently: “I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it’s a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

webTitle: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods

fields.headline: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods
fields.trailText: Ottawa’s ‘focused response’ to levies imposed by Donald Trump on Canadian products comes after trade talks collapsed last week
fields.bodyText: Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US. In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices. The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year. The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House. The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9bn) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper. The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US. In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”. The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war. “You have power,” she said. The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months. Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around. Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US. Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!” Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”. Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

webTitle: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it | Arwa Mahdawi

fields.headline: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it
fields.trailText: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
fields.bodyText: Despite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking about Abdul El-Sayed’s biceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot of fitness content in his campaign. I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has a serious image problem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal. “Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News website Axios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed ‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”. Fox News would appear to reluctantly agree with the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.” Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewole proclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.” Sex sells too: it’s well established that voters around the world prefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016 study found that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study by the Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.) Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960, 70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedy in the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup. You can quibble with the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In his memoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.” In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? webTitle: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan
fields.trailText: US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself
fields.bodyText: Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges. Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. What did the dissenting judges say? In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”. How have rights organisations reacted? The president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Derrick Johnson, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it and we have to protect the rights we do have within it … they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote.” Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel Donald Trump has announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbours with traditionally strong economic ties. The US president said Canada had been “ripping off” the US for years and that it was “among the worst Nations in the World to deal with”. How has Canada reacted? The country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff,” he said. Carney has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”, and said Canada could not accept any proposed trade deal that would weaken French language protections. US strikes vessel in eastern Pacific, killing two people in first attack in months The US military has struck a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking. US Southern Command (SouthCom) said it had “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. SouthCom did not provide evidence of the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking. Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series since the Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US. Numerous reports, however, indicate the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country. US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do. It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally. Iran vowed retaliation against any country that takes part in the US-led isolation campaign. Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war. In other news … Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants. The country continues to deal with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes. US healthcare officials said a food-poisoning outbreak tied to alfalfa sprouts had sickened people in at least 15 states. Target has pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature. A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said. An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post to rehire the high-profile opinion columnist Karen Attiah, who was fired abruptly last September over social media comments about Charlie Kirk. Stat of the day: Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000 asylum seekers’ visas A Department of State spokesperson said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”. Associated Press put the number of people potentially involved at as many as 200,000, which would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history. Culture pick: Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn before. Don’t miss this: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold Everybody loves seals and sea lions – the dogs of the ocean – but in Australia there are fears that bird flu has jumped species and could endanger them. Lisa Cox investigates. … or this: Why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer who did things her own way. Climate check: Nevada files lawsuit challenging federal plan for Colorado River revival Nevada has filed a federal lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s plan for the imperilled Colorado River, which threatens to cut roughly 20% of the water supplied to lower basin states – Nevada, Arizona and California – over the next two years. It could become the first of many court battles over the waterway that supplies 40 million people, dozens of tribes and 5.5m acres of farmland across the American west. webTitle: US building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China in AI boom, analysis finds

fields.headline: US building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China in AI boom, analysis finds
fields.trailText: There has been a 76% increase in under-construction gas-fired projects amid ‘frenzy’ to build more datacenters
fields.bodyText: The US has surged ahead of China in the building of new gas-fired power generation, largely to feed a boom in artificial intelligence (AI) that is adding vast amounts of planet-heating emissions, a new analysis has found. For decades, China’s rapid economic growth has seen it outpace the US in the addition of new gas power generation but a recent “frenzy” in datacenter construction for AI has reversed this, said Global Energy Monitor (Gem) in its new report. The US is now building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China, and more than any other country in the world, after a stunning 76% increase in under-construction projects in the first half of this year. When adding announced and pre-construction projects, the US is building nearly three times as much as its fellow global economic powerhouse. Since January, gas power capacity in overall development in the US has ballooned by 50%, rising from 252GW to 378GW – a third of the global total. If all of these projects are ultimately built, the US will increase its gas fleet by about two-thirds at a capital cost of more than $647bn, Gem found. Around half of the new capacity is directly tied to a rash of upcoming datacenters that require a huge amount of electricity to handle the increased demand from AI. Using gas, a fossil fuel that is dangerously overheating our planet, rather than renewables to power this glut of new datacenters threatens to increase US power emissions by as much as 20%, according to one estimate. “Six months ago, China had more gas plants under construction but that has now flipped,” said Jenny Martos, a project manager at Global Energy Monitor. “There has been an enormous surge in datacenter proposals powered by gas in the past year and the climate implications of that is huge. Building all of this gas for AI locks in decades of pollution and it is also locking in dependence on a volatile fuel cost, which will get passed down to rate payers.” Donald Trump and others in his administration have repeatedly claimed that China, the world’s largest carbon polluter, is expanding its fossil fuel use so much that any emissions cuts by the US would be futile. The president has said of China that “their air is dirty, and it drifts over to us”. But the rush of new infrastructure for AI, along with the Trump administration’s demolition of environmental regulations and China’s rapid adoption of clean energy, is changing this equation. US spending on power plants fueled by coal and gas will outstrip that of China for the first time in decades, the International Energy Agency has forecast. The stampede by tech companies, such as Google, Open AI and Amazon, to build datacenters has contributed to a backlog of the most efficient gas turbines used for accompanying power plants. This has led several companies, including Elon Musk’s xAI, to quickly switch to smaller, less efficient turbines which are more heavily polluting. Concerns over the climate crisis, rising power bills, tax breaks for AI companies and water shortages – two-thirds of more than 800 planned datacenters are located in drought-stricken areas – has fueled mounting local opposition to data center construction. A recent poll by Heatmap found that three-quarters of Americans do not want to live next to a datacenter, a huge increase in opposition in the past year. Dozens of cities and counties have placed restrictions on new datacenters, with New York in July becoming the first state to enact a temporary ban on new hyper-scale datacenter permitting and construction. Despite this backlash, which could well hurt Republicans in the November midterm elections, the Trump administration has championed the building of new datacenters and eliminated environmental reviews in order to speed them up. Trump said this month that “data centers could be bigger than oil” and state governors should cut taxes to encourage them. “Frankly, communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake because there’s plenty of communities that want them,” Trump said in separate remarks to his former lawyer Michael Cohen last week. “Because it means jobs, and it means tremendous tax revenue coming into the towns and cities that take them.”

webTitle: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?

fields.headline: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
fields.trailText: Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
fields.bodyText: In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting “tariffs and war”. If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate. “When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas,” Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. “That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I’m a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn’t have got in the race if I didn’t.” The founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party’s primary, though Marshall is still favored to win. For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress’s upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they’ve named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so. The US president’s slumping approval ratings and the Iran war’s impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats’ chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin. This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a “blue wave” of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win. Asked what he thought of Schumer’s prediction, Hamilton said: “I don’t agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I’m telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don’t care what else happens across the country.” No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber’s Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since. Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor’s mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state. “Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there’s something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won’t pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor,” said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka. But Hamilton’s experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for “a very competitive race” against Marshall. “What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He’s been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years,” he said. Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump’s debunked claims of fraud in that year’s presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration’s funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment. Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. He mulled running as an independent, but ultimately filed as a Democrat, saying he was concerned that he’d split the vote if he wasn’t in a party and agreed with its views on “healthcare, education [and] social safety nets”. “Those are things that matter a lot to me, and my faith leads in that direction,” he said. A self-described “moderate or independent-minded Democrat”, his campaign recently released an ad where Hamilton likens Kansas’s position in the middle of the country to his own approach to the politics that would await him in Washington DC. Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being “a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas”, and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he’d put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m. The senator recently called his opponent a “megachurch pastor that’s too woke for Kansas”, the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context. Like so much in his career, Hamilton’s chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as “a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas” and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran. “The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas,” Slattery said. “It’s the bottom line.” • This article was amended on 26 August 2026. A previous version described Adam Hamilton as the founder of the largest Methodist denomination in the US. He is the founder of the largest United Methodist congregation in the US.

webTitle: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman head to South Carolina’s Senate runoff

fields.headline: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman head to South Carolina’s Senate runoff
fields.trailText: Republican nominee to face Democrat Annie Andrews in midterm after rushed campaigns for Lindsey Graham’s seat
fields.bodyText: Reese Boyd, the chair of the Horry county Republican party marveled on Monday afternoon at how little time Senator Darline Graham and Representative Ralph Norman have had to campaign for the Senate primary: “This is not the normal way of things.” “This is something that usually lasts at least, you know, the better part of a year,” he said. “People normally spend the better part of 18 months getting ready for it. Who knows? This may be the right way to do it? Who knows.” On Tuesday, Graham and Norman will conclude a 45-day campaign sprint that began with the unexpected death of Lindsey Graham in July. Henry McMaster, the state’s Republican governor, appointed Graham’s sister, Darline, to serve out the remainder of his term. Because Lindsey Graham had won the Republican primary, state law required a fresh election to replace him on the ballot in November. The winner will face Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic candidate, in a state where Democrats haven’t won statewide in two decades. Many observers had expected Darline Graham to serve in a caretaker role while South Carolina’s political leadership staged a political knife fight for a rare shot at a US Senate seat. Instead, the political newcomer – a career civil servant who led the state’s commission for the blind – surprised the political establishment and announced her decision to stand for a full term – with the encouragement and backing of Donald Trump. Graham overcame concerns about her lack of legislative experience earlier this month, claiming the top spot to advance to the 25 August runoff, from a sprawling, 10-candidate Republican field. “I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham said recently, referring to a well-publicized gaffe in a debate last week with Norman, where she responded to a question about defense policy by saying that military stuff “is not my thing”. Norman has pounced on her comment, highlighting it as an example of her unreadiness for the role. “Imagine if I went to [head football coach] Dabo Swinney at Clemson and any of the coaches and said: ‘Look, I got a prospect I want you to look at, and I want them to,” Norman said to the Associated Press. “‘They can start. I want you to sign them up. They can start for the next six years.’ ‘What’s the qualifications?’ ‘They’re kin to Tom Brady.’ Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here.” Lindsey Graham had built a reputation as a foreign policy hawk, who championed the US war against Iran and rallied support for Ukraine in its defense against the Russian invasion. Darline Graham has framed her candidacy as a way to “carry my brother Lindsey’s legacy”. Since being sworn in as his successor last month, she has voted along party lines, but little else is known about her politics. Norman, who has been called the most conservative member of the US House, is running billboard advertisements on South Carolina highways that say “Voting for Ralph Norman is MAGA” as an answer to Trump’s endorsement of Graham. Trump framed his support for Darline Graham as the repayment of a favor to his late friend, Lindsey Graham. “I asked her to do this,” Trump said on Friday in a campaign stop in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. “I said, ‘Darline, you gotta do it.’ ‘Cause everyone loves her, everyone respects her. I’ve known her, through Lindsey … I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me. That does not make me happy. I’m not happy about that.” But by elevating a relative political unknown whose primary appeal to voters is her promise to follow the president’s lead, Trump has offered one more high-profile test of his influence over Republican voters before the midterm elections in 10 weeks, a point he made explicit at the rally on Friday. “The problem that we have is, they say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come and they don’t vote for senators, congressmen and other Republicans,” the president said. “And that these people, they’re running, they’re great. But Trump isn’t actually on the ballot. So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote.”

webTitle: I once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches down | Bryan Armen Graham

fields.headline: I once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches down
fields.trailText: Nearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, Kanter is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a national punchline
fields.bodyText: Nine years ago, I watched Enes Kanter ask America to take him in. It was May 2017, inside the National Basketball Players Association’s offices in midtown Manhattan. Kanter had just returned from a frightening detention at Bucharest airport, where Romanian border police told him Turkey had canceled his passport. He’d just turned 25, an NBA center with a green card and no country he could safely call home. “I’m open for adoption,” he joked from the head of a table in a nondescript conference room, addressing a dozen reporters hastily summoned by his manager. Then he turned serious: “My next move is to just become an American citizen.” The previous 48 hours had unfolded like a John le Carré thriller. Kanter said his manager woke him at 2.30am in Jakarta where he’d been hosting a basketball clinic because Indonesian security forces were looking for him. He hurried to Singapore, then Frankfurt, only to be stopped in Romania. He feared being sent to Turkey, where he had grown up and whose national team he had represented. There, he said, no one might hear from him again. Department of Homeland Security officials and lawyers for the Oklahoma City Thunder and the players’ union helped get him back to the United States. Sitting in that room that Monday morning, I saw someone who had already paid a steep cost for the right to speak truth to power. Kanter called Recep Tayyip Erdoğan the “Hitler of our century”. He recounted daily death threats, a family placed in jeopardy by his opposition to Erdoğan and support for the president’s exiled rival, Fethullah Gülen, and parents he had stopped calling because he feared the government was tapping their phones. He said his father, Mehmet, a university professor, had been spat on at a supermarket. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” he told us. The reprisals only widened. Turkey issued warrants for Kanter and later sought an Interpol Red Notice and his extradition. He skipped NBA trips abroad, including a Knicks game in London, because he feared detention or assassination. His father was dismissed, detained and charged with membership in a terrorist organization before his eventual acquittal in 2020. In 2021, Kanter finally became an American citizen and legally added Freedom to his name. You didn’t have to squint hard to make out the symbolism. The dissident Turkey tried to render voiceless and stateless had found both an adopted home and a protected platform. On Sunday night, I found myself thinking about the young man from that news conference – and wondering what became of him. Back then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attention. Kanter was sitting courtside at the Chicago Sky’s game against the Indiana Fever in a shirt reading: “WOMAN noun. adult human female.” He had joined a rally outside the arena in support of Sophie Cunningham, the Fever guard who opposes transgender participation in women’s sports. In recent weeks, Kanter had also declared himself eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft, claiming to identify as a woman and posting workout videos about beginning his “transition”. (League sources have since said he is not eligible to play and dismissed his declaration as a publicity stunt the WNBA would not “give oxygen” to.) The crudity of the attempted reductio ad absurdum was matched only by the breathlessness of the response across the Maga right, where Kanter’s stunt was greeted as an intellectual masterstroke: BRILLIANT, GOT ‘EM, CHECKMATE. Fox News has not merely covered Kanter’s bit uncritically; it has plainly participated in the mockery. Take the premise of transgender inclusion, distort it into the spectacle of a former NBA player treating womanhood as a debating prop, and wait for the audience to laugh. Yet Kanter exposed no contradiction. The punchline was simply the existence of transgender people. No player assigned male at birth has ever competed in the WNBA. Whatever legitimate questions exist about eligibility rules, competitive balance and the place of biology in elite sport can be discussed without reducing them to a spectacle designed to humiliate those at the center of the debate. Kanter’s stunt depends on the idea that gender identity is inherently fraudulent and that trans women are simply opportunistic men waiting to invade women’s spaces. It has done nothing to clarify policy. It has merely turned a vulnerable minority into content – including many trans fans who have long regarded the 30-year-old league as one of the few places in professional sport where they belong. At a moment when ESPN’s WNBA coverage is averaging 1.4 million viewers, up 16% from the same point last season, Kanter’s stunt has hijacked a feelgood story about the league’s growth and made a phantom threat the focus instead. The invasion rhetoric carries a bitter irony. The WNBA is not being overrun by trans women but by straight men who cannot let women have a flourishing league of their own without mocking it, manufacturing controversy and making themselves the story. Some of loudest voices posing as defenders of female athletes openly ridicule and try to humiliate them for laughs, in some cases through sexualized stunts. There is something almost pitiable about men squandering their energy and influence on belittling women whose discipline, sacrifice and extraordinary achievement have carried them to the highest level of their profession. Misogyny has simply put on the costume of concern. In Kanter’s case, this was not simply a lone provocateur wandering into an arena. According to Talking Points Memo, the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute (AFPI) promoted Kanter’s arrival, circulated footage of his ejection and began selling a $45 “Let Freedom Play” sweatshirt featuring him in a mock-up of the WNBA logo. An AFPI executive was seated a few rows behind him, although the organization did not answer questions about whether it bought his courtside seat. Kanter, who attended the 2024 State of the Union as House speaker Mike Johnson’s guest and has said he plans to run for Congress in 2028, has political ambitions of his own. Whether or not there is a formal arrangement, the transaction is visible enough: Kanter lends the campaign the credibility of an 11-year NBA veteran and supplies a spectacle in which transgender people are the bait, while an organization embedded in Trump’s political network converts those assets into attention, merchandise and political capital. If it keeps voters staring at a nonexistent threat to the WNBA instead of the breathtaking corruption engulfing the administration in the run-up to the November midterms, the stunt has done its real work. Late in the third quarter of Sunday’s contest, Natasha Cloud, one of the most uncompromising athlete-activists of her generation, finally took the rage bait. The Sky guard approached Kanter, yelling and pointing in his direction. Kanter stood, spread his arms and stepped on to the court before security intervened. As he was escorted away, he stopped near the basket to argue his case, then stretched out his shirt and tried to draw a response from the crowd. He had arrived ready to provoke and left performing martyrdom. Kanter did not suddenly discover the uses of spectacle on Sunday. In 2020, after marching with Black Lives Matter protesters in Boston, he told the Guardian that athletes should use their platforms “to spread good, and to spread the truth”. He had long understood publicity as a political tool, and with good reason: he believed international pressure helped secure his father’s acquittal. The difference is what the performance now serves. None of this diminishes the courage Kanter showed in opposing Erdoğan. The offer of US citizenship is not a contract for ideological obedience. Human rights are not a prize withdrawn when their beneficiary later behaves immorally, nor does surviving persecution bind anyone to a prescribed worldview. But suffering does not automatically make a person generous, either. And Kanter, more than most, should understand the mechanics of dehumanization: how a powerful movement marks a minority as dangerous, treats its identity as illegitimate and converts real human beings into totems of social decay. The scale of Erdoğan’s repression and an American culture-war stunt are not equivalent. The moral reflex behind them – identifying people with less power and making public sport of their vulnerability – should have been instantly recognizable to him. The least cynical reading, perhaps charitable to a fault, is that Kanter can recognize this kind of othering only when he is its target. US citizenship gave Kanter what he asked for in that Manhattan conference room: safety, a home and the freedom to speak without Erdoğan deciding the consequences. That freedom includes the right to make a cruel spectacle of himself, but it does not exempt the spectacle from judgment. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” Kanter said in 2017. I believed him then. On Sunday, he used that voice to make other innocent people feel smaller. What a waste.

webTitle: Gavin Newsom says California will sue Trump administration again to block ‘Orwellian rules’ meant to curb mail-in voting – as it happened

fields.headline: Gavin Newsom says California will sue Trump administration again to block ‘Orwellian rules’ meant to curb mail-in voting – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: The US supreme court lifted one of two injunctions that block the Trump administration from pressing ahead with a sweeping effort to restrict mail voting The court’s decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”, justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote in a blistering dissent. The NAACP, which sued in April to block the order to restrict mail-in voting, said that Republicans are trying to make it harder to vote in November because they “know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election”. The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum status in the United States, according to US state department documents obtained by the Associated Press. Donald Trump responded to criticism of his new tariffs on Canadian imports from the premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, by comparing him unfavorably to his late brother, Rob Ford, a former mayor of Toronto best known for smoking crack. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US has begun an “unprecedented” sanctions campaign against Iran “and its enablers”. While the US supreme court on Monday lifted one of two injunctions that block the Trump administration from pressing ahead with a sweeping federal power grab over mail voting, a number of legal experts have pointed out that no changes can be made while the second injunction remains in place. The real action, they note, will come in legal challenges to a US Postal Service rule that would allow it to not deliver ballots in states that refuse to hand over lists of eligible voters, in line with an executive order issued in March by Donald Trump. “Please don’t overreact to Roberts Court decision on the contemplated USPS ballot moves,” Norm Eisen, a former ethics adviser in the Obama White House and a founder of the legacy advocacy group Democracy Defenders Action, wrote on social media. “They simply held that the injunction came too early in the process, before there was a final rule … Now we HAVE a final rule & we will litigate it. I’m as confident in our arguments here as in any of our cases!” Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown University law professor, wrote in his newsletter: “Late Friday night, the U.S. Postal Service (finally) released the ‘Final Rule’ that was supposed to be published by the end of July that purports to implement Trump’s executive order. It’s that rule, not the executive order itself, that would be the basis for the USPS messing with mail-in ballots come October and November.” Vladeck suggests that, as soon as Tuesday, a federal judge could block the new USPS rule on mail ballots, which essentially requires states to hand over lists of eligible voters to the federal government before any mail ballots can be delivered. That rule is scheduled to go into effect on Wednesday. Something called the Purcell principle, which dictates that courts should not change the rules on how people vote too close to an election, could come in to play, Vladeck writes. With mail ballots set to go out to North Carolina voters in the military or abroad at the end of next week, the supreme court’s conservative majority could invoke the Purcell principle as an excuse to strike down any legal challenge to the new USPS rule as coming “too close to the election”. “That’s a genuine concern, and given the Court’s own repeated transgressions of the Purcell principle earlier this term in Texas, Louisiana, and Alabama, to hide behind it to allow the USPS Final Rule to go into effect would be as indefensible and anti-democratic a ruling as the Court has handed down in a very long time,” Vladeck argues. The two dozen plaintiffs that lost at the supreme court on Monday, 23 states and the District of Columbia that sued to block the Trump administration from implementing sweeping restrictions on mail voting, have lined up to express outrage and their determination to fight on in the courts. Officials in Oregon, which has conducted its elections entirely by mail since 1998, vowed on Monday to take legal action if the US Postal Service or any other federal agency “unlawfully takes steps to interfere with mail voting”. “We’re not going to let Donald Trump interfere in our elections—and we’re certainly not going to let him decide who gets a ballot and who doesn’t,” Oregon’s attorney general Dan Rayfield said. “Today’s court decision is a temporary setback, nothing more. This fight is far from over.” The state’s top elections official, secretary of state Tobias Read, said the midterms “will proceed as planned this November, free from any illegal federal interference”. “President Trump’s directive to the United States Postal Service is unconstitutional and an assault on our democracy and designed to silence voters,” Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, said. “Oregon has been conducting elections by mail-in voting safely and securely for decades. My message to the President is clear: keep your hands off our elections.” California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, said on Monday that his state would sue the Trump administration again to block federal changes to mail voting, after the US supreme court ruled that a previous suit was filed too early in the process by his state and 22 others. “California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented,” Newsom posted. Newsom also highlighted two new proposed state laws that would make it a crime to interfere with the delivery of mail ballots. In a press release, Newsom added that he and the California legislature “are doubling down to ensure California continues to defend democracy as new threats from Donald Trump and his election-rigging allies emerge”. Two draft laws would establish three new felonies under California state law, punishable by up to four years in prison. One of the laws would prohibit anyone “from seizing or causing the seizure of ballots, election records, or certified voting technology before election results are certified”, and blocks “any person with authority from directing someone in their supervision to do the same”. The second law makes it a felony “for a person in a position with authority” to direct another person “to interfere with a ballot’s delivery to a voter or return to the local elections official”. That same legislation would make it a misdemeanor to interfere with “the delivery of a vote by mail ballot to a voter”. Rick Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, points out on his Election Law Blog that the supreme court on Monday only lifted one of two lower-court orders that blocked the Trump administration from implementing its planned restrictions on mail voting. The other injunction, not ruled on by the court yet, still stops the US Postal Service from implementing a new rule that would allow it to refuse to deliver ballots mailed by voters who are not on a list approved by the federal government. Hasen also observes that it is “just weird” that the court issued its opinion on Monday, in which it ruled that the states that sued to block the implementation of new federal rules around mail voting should have waited until the USPS proposed a new rule to do what Trump directed. While it is true that the 23 states and Washington DC filed suit before the USPS issued its new rule, the final rule was posted online late Friday, and is set to take effect this week if the court lifts the both injunctions. Monday’s supreme court decision, Hasen added, “just postpones any kind of ruling on the merits, but a week or two, when we will be even closer to the election and it will be impossible for states to comply with some of the rules that will come out”. As the North Carolina board of elections notes on its website: “Voting in the 2026 election officially begins on Sept. 4, with the initial sending of absentee ballots to voters who requested them.” The president of the NAACP, which sued Donald Trump in April to block his order to restrict mail-in voting, denounced the supreme court decision that allows the order to be implemented, despite claims that it is illegal and unconstitutional. The NAACP president, Derrick Johnson, said in a statement: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever, guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it, and we have to protect the rights we do have within it. Those in power know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election, and so they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote. Trump’s order has nothing to do with election integrity. It has everything to do with maintaining power at all costs.” The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States, according to US state department documents obtained by the Associated Press. According to the documents and unnamed sources who spoke to the AP, the state department plans to announce within weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, whose holders have sought or are now seeking asylum. A state department spokesperson told the news agency it is working with the Department of Homeland Security on the push. “We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” the spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said. Pigott declined to confirm the number of visas that might be revoked, since “as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.” The US supreme court’s decision on Monday that the Trump administration can move ahead with plans to restrict mail-in voting “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”, justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote in a blistering dissent. While the court’s unsigned opinion, from the six Republican-appointed justices, did not say that an executive order signed by Donald Trump to limit mail voting was legal, Jackson argued that permitting the administration to push ahead with changes, including a plan for the US Postal Service (USPS) to refuse to deliver ballots from voters not on a pre-approved list of eligible voters created by the federal government, “contributes to pre-election chaos instead of quashing it”. “Our Constitution expressly delegates the power to conduct federal elections to the States,” Jackson wrote. In a 31 March 2026 executive order, Trump “attempted to alter this longstanding, constitutionally assigned structure” that “requires a fundamental overhaul of the States’ existing mail-in ballot systems—changing from a state-administered process to one in which the Federal Government controls who gets a ballot and whose vote counts”. Jackson went on to accuse her conservative colleagues of “a stunning misinterpretation of the factual record” in their claim that a lower court had engaged in speculation that the United States Postal Service would change its rules to refuse to deliver mail ballots in states that did not turn over their voter rolls to the federal government. As Jackson notes, the USPS has proposed a change to its rules, which is scheduled to take effect this week. “In the end, though, what makes today’s ruling so off-base is the Court’s lack of situational awareness regarding this equitable judgment,” Jackson writes in her conclusion. “Taking its eye off the ball, the majority misses the Government’s actual objective: to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.” The US supreme court on Monday granted the Trump administration’s request to lift a lower court order that had blocked it from implementing Donald Trump’s executive order to restrict mail-in voting. The decision by the court’s conservative majority, with its liberal members dissenting, appears to leave room for additional court challenges that could prevent the implementation of the new restrictions in time for the upcoming midterm elections in November, with some states beginning to send mail ballots to voters in just a few weeks. The case could be one of multiple voting-related challenges before the justices. The justice department had filed an emergency appeal asking the high court to allow work on implementing the changes before the midterms. Trump’s executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the US Postal Service (USPS) to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists. The USPS is prepared to publish a new rule this week to implement that change. As we mentioned earlier, Donald Trump quickly got personal in response to criticism of his new tariffs on Canadian imports from the conservative premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, by comparing him unfavorably to his late brother, Rob Ford, a former rightwing mayor of Toronto. Writing on social media, Trump called the Ontario leader a “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive” version of his brother. What makes the US president’s enthusiastic praise for the late Rob Ford is that he was best known outside Canada for one thing: having been caught on video smoking crack while serving as mayor. While the video was not made public until after Rob Ford’s death in 2016, he admitted in 2013 that he had smoked crack, “probably in one of my drunken stupors” in 2012. The same year, the Ford brothers met Trump at the opening of a new Trump International Hotel and Tower in Toronto. During Trump’s successful campaign for the Republican nomination for president in 2016, Doug Ford expressed delight that Trump had used one of his brother’s slogans. “It’s a real tribute and a real honour,” Doug Ford told the Toronto Sun. “Full disclosure, I like Trump,” he added. “He’s not part of the Washington establishment or the Washington elites ... I wouldn’t underestimate him.” By last year, Doug Ford’s affection for Trump had waned so much that, as Ontario’s leader, he paid to have a television ad against Trump’s tariffs, featuring anti-tariff comments from Ronald Reagan, broadcast during the World Series, which infuriated Trump. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows that public approval for the war with Iran has dropped to its lowest level since the conflict’s early days at the end of February. Now, only 31% of Americans surveyed support military action in Iran, which is down from 34% earlier this month. Notably, fewer Americans who identify as Republican support the war, according to the poll. That number now sits at 69%, compared to 77% in March. This comes at a time when Donald Trump’s own approval rating hovers at a new low of 33%, according to recent polling. Scott Bessent announced today that the US has begun an “unprecedented” sanctions campaign against Iran “and its enablers”. A number of countries stand to face secondary sanctions, according to the treasury secretary. However, he did not say whether those, like China or Russia, would be impacted. He also did not set out a timeline for those countries to end doing business with Iran. “We know who they are, they know who they are, so when the hammer of US treasury actions falls upon them they will have no one to blame but themselves,” Bessent said, describing the new wave of sanctions as “economic asphyxiation” of the Iranian regime and “no one should test our resolve”. Meanwhile, Donald Trump has threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50% today, after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down last week. On Truth Social, the US president blasted Canada and said the new duties will go into effect on 1 January 2027. “On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” Trump wrote. This escalation comes after Canadian prime minister Mark Carney rejected the latest deal on Saturday, after Trump previously slapped a 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports – ranging from hockey equipment to electronics. In response, Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” he said from Quebec. “But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” he continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.” Trump, however, continued a war of words with Ontario premier Doug Ford, who he said was displaying “lots of bluster”. Trump called Ford the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive” version of his brother Rob Ford, the former mayor of Toronto. Earlier, the Ontario premier said that Canada must “throw everything and the kitchen sink” at the US in the wake of Trump’s tariff announcement. “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so he [Trump] has a lot of room to kiss my ass,” Ford told reporters on Monday. Earlier, ahead of Trump announcing his latest threat to implement 50% tariffs on Canadian cars and auto parts, Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, said that Canada is ultimately responsible for the collapsed talks over the weekend to reach a deal on the duties between the two countries and longtime allies. “We set about to finalize it, and then in the last hours, I think there were things that the Canadians just – you know, they wanted more,” Greer said today in an interview with CNBC. “They wanted more and we weren’t prepared to do that.” Donald Trump said there is “lots of bluster” coming from Ontario premier Doug Ford, as the two engaged in a war of words on Monday. The US president called Ford the “less charismatic, intelligent and overall unimpressive” version of his brother Rob Ford, the former mayor of Toronto. Earlier today, Doug Ford said that Canada must “throw everything and the kitchen sink” at the US after Trump threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian auto parts and cars to 50%. “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so he [Trump] has a lot of room to kiss my ass,” Ford told reporters today. “The red states – we’re gonna hit hard,” the premier said. “You think an insult from him [Trump] hurts me? Bring it on, buddy. You’re a loser.” On Truth Social, Trump remained bullish. “America has been carrying Canada for decades, but no longer! The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada,” he wrote. “Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive – It’s where they get all of their money and, because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford, they will not be allowed to keep taking advantage of the United States – Their key to survival.” By referring to Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, as a “governor”, Trump continues to brand the country as a “state” in the US. Earlier, in Maine, vice-president JD Vance repeated a similar posture. “Remember, much of the Electricity, Oil, and Gas that Canada gets is transported through the U.S.A. Someone should get these clowns to “fall in line” or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!” Trump added. All US immigration officers working for a key anti-fraud unit have been reassigned by Donald Trump’s administration to focus on screening South African refugees and alleged “unlawful” voters. Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS) immigration officers have been shifted full-time on to two “high-priority” initiatives, according to internal correspondence seen by the Guardian, leaving US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) unable to provide officers to train asylum officers in “the near future”. USCIS is inside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has led the president’s immigration crackdown during his second term. The processing of asylum claims has largely ground to a halt during Trump’s administration, leaving many seeking asylum in limbo. “All FDNS IOs [immigration officers] have been reassigned full-time to one of two high-priority USCIS initiatives (South African refugee screening and unlawful voter screening),” an internal message, sent on Monday, said. “Because of this, we will not have the ability to assign IO’s [immigration officers] to the training portfolio for the near future.” USCIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. FDNS is the USCIS unit responsible for detecting fraud and national security concerns in immigration benefit applications, including asylum claims. Its officers work with asylum offices to identify cases requiring further investigation, refer matters to law enforcement, and help asylum officers identify potential fraud and other red flags. The reassignment marks a significant diversion of FDNS personnel. The message addresses only the agency’s ability to provide officers for asylum officer training; it does not say whether routine FDNS screening of pending asylum applications has also slowed or stopped. A disruption to training would limit specialized instruction for asylum officers, and a broader slowdown in casework screening would have more direct consequences for pending applications. The Guardian has not independently confirmed whether routine asylum screening has been affected. When asked why the US treasury department is not implementing sanctions immediately, Bessent said that it was to give nations who conduct business with Iran the “opportunity to remedy bad behavior”. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said. “We believe that it’s important to level set and give people a cure period. But they should know that will move very quickly, and that we are serious.” Notably, during his press conference today, Scott Bessent didn’t specify which countries would be targeted by secondary sanctions, even when asked by reporters whether China – the largest importer of Iranian oil – would be impacted. While Bessent said that “quiet diplomacy” is the best way to engage with countries who still maintain trade relationships with Iran, this latest move is an attempt to show that “no one is above” sanctions. “We know who they are, they know who they are, so when the hammer of US treasury actions falls upon them they will have no one to blame but themselves,” Bessent said.
